Option A matches this. Option C puts the kitchen in the sleeping group, which is wrong. Option B describes a corridor layout rather than a grouped plan. Option D puts the bedrooms in the day area, which is wrong.

Answer: A

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: When should the entrance hall of a dwelling be enclosed with an inner door to act as a wind lobby, and in which case is this unnecessary?
options: Only when the entrance faces the prevailing wind from the south
Only in residential buildings of more than five storeys with lifts
Always, regardless of the entrance type or local weather conditions
When the entrance leads directly to the open air; a stair shaft entrance already gives wind protection
source: if the entrance is into a stair shaft, then this can provide wind protection
The entrance hall should be enclosed where the entrance leads directly to the open air with an inner door (wind lobby function).
context:
Entrance
The entrance is the face of a house, where visitors gain their first impression. A multitude of functions have to be practically arranged and appropriately designed → ①. If the entrance is into the open air, it should be protected from the prevailing wind direction if possible. If weather conditions are unfavourable, a lobby is also recommended to prevent wind blowing through → p. 136 (if the entrance is into a stair shaft, then this can provide wind protection).

Entrance hall
The entrance hall should be enclosed where the entrance leads directly to the open air with an inner door (wind lobby function). It should also offer sufficient room for a lot of moving around → ④. This is where reception, greeting, taking off and putting on coats, and taking leave all take place, but also offers the first orientation for the visitor → ① – ③. Countless objects therefore have to be arranged practically yet tidily in this limited space → ⑤, ⑥. The most important communal areas like the kitchen, WC and staircase should be directly accessible from the entrance hall.

Entrance
The entrance is the face of a house, where visitors gain their first impression. A multitude of functions have to be practically arranged and appropriately designed → ①. If the entrance is into the open air, it should be protected from the prevailing wind direction if possible. If weather conditions are unfavourable, a lobby is also recommended to prevent wind blowing through → p. 136 (if the entrance is into a stair shaft, then this can provide wind protection).

answer.text:
This looks like it comes from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre. The relevant passage says the entrance hall (Diele) of a dwelling should be closed off by an inner door to serve as a wind lobby (Windfang) when the entrance leads directly to the open air. This is not needed when the entrance is from a stair shaft, which already gives wind protection.

Option D matches that passage.

Answer: D

question.text: According to DIN 277, the gross built volume is the sum of the floor areas of all levels multiplied by the relevant height. Between which surfaces is that height measured?
options: From the underside of one structural slab to the underside of the next
From the top of the floor covering to the top of the floor covering of the next level
From the top of the structural slab to the underside of the suspended ceiling
From the top of the floor covering to the underside of the ceiling
source: The gross built volume is the sum of the floor areas of all levels multiplied by the relevant height (measured between top of floor covering and top of floor covering of the next level
context: …lding services, such as utility connection room, accessible shafts, etc.) and the traffic area (e.g. stairwells, corridors, lift shafts, escape balconies etc.). The gross built volume is the sum of the floor areas of all levels multiplied by the relevant height (measured between top of floor covering and top of floor covering of the next level, in the basement from the underside of the constructional structural invert in the roof to the top of the roof covering, without external stairs, light wells, roof overhangs, dormer windows, chimneys, etc.). The net built volume is the net floor area multiplied by the relevant clear ceiling height.

…etween the external dimensions at floor height. The net floor area is the usable floor area between the building elements (without door and window openings, cut-outs and niches) measured at floor level. The net floor area is the sum of the usable area (area which serves the building’s intended purpose), the technical function area (rooms for building services, such as utility connection room, accessible shafts, etc.) and the traffic area (e.g. stairwells, corridors, lift shafts, escape balconies etc.). The gross built volume is the sum of the floor areas of all levels multiplied by the relevant height (measured between top of floor covering and top of floor covering of the next level, in the basement from the underside of the constructional structural invert in the roof to the top of the roof covering, without external stairs, light wells, roof overhangs, dormer windows, chimneys, etc.). The net built volume is the net floor area multiplied by the relevant clear ceiling height.

meta.title: DIN 277 建筑体积（总体积与净体积）

answer.text:
DIN 277 (older version 1987) defines Brutto-Rauminhalt (BRI) as the volume of the building body multiplied by the heights: from the upper surface of the lowest floor (Oberkante Fußboden/ Oberkante Boden) to the upper surface of the roof construction/top of the roof covering. For intermediate levels, the height is measured from the top of the floor to the top of the floor above. In the 2005 and 2016 versions, BRI is the volume of the building body bounded by the outer surfaces of the enclosing building elements, with the lower boundary being the underside of the lowest floor structure.

The question asks for the height between surfaces of floors, and the "relevant height" from floor to floor is best matched by option B: from the top of the floor covering to the top of the floor covering of the next level.

Option D describes the clear room height, which is used for the net room volume rather than the gross volume.

Answer: B

question.text: Under the German housing area regulation (2003), from which reference surface is a room's floor area measured?
options: From the external faces of the enclosing walls
Clear dimensions from the face of the building components' cladding
From the unfinished structural faces of the walls
source: The floor area of a room is determined from the clearance space between building components and starts from the face of the cladding of the building component
context:
Housing area regulation
The 'Regulation for the calculation of the housing area' of 25/11/2003 is used to work out the area of houses and flats for the purpose of the Law to Subsidise House Building. The area of a house or flat includes the floor area of all rooms which belong exclusively to the house or, in the case of a residential home the areas intended for the sole use of the owner → 2.

The floor area of a room is determined from the clearance space between building components and starts from the face of the cladding of the building component → ③. The floor area is measured in the completed room, or can be calculated from a suitable construction drawing. Floor areas are calculated according to → ④.

meta.title: 住宅面积的计入范围与净尺寸量法

answer.text:
The Wohnflächenverordnung (WoFlV) of 2003 specifies in §3 that the floor area is determined from the clear dimensions between the finished surfaces of the enclosing components, meaning the plastered or clad faces. The older DIN 283 and the II. Berechnungsverordnung also measured on the plastered surfaces, in contrast to DIN 277, which measures from the structural faces.

WoFlV §3 (Ermittlung der Grundfläche): "(1) Die Grundfläche ist nach den lichten Maßen zwischen den Bauteilen zu ermitteln; Vorlagen vor Wänden bis 15 cm sind nicht... Bei der Ermittlung der Grundfläche ist von den fertigen Maßen auszugehen" — and "Wird die Grundfläche nach den Bauzeichnungen ermittelt, ist von den Rohbaumaßen auszugehen. Von den ermittelten Maßen ist ein Abzug von 3 % für Putz vorzunehmen" (this is §3 para 2).

The question asks which reference surface applies, and the best-fitting option is B: clear dimensions from the face of the building components' cladding (that is, the finished surfaces). Option C describes the unfinished structural faces, which is only the fallback when measuring from drawings, and then with a 3% deduction for plaster.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In dwelling design, to which compass directions are parents' bedrooms and children's bedrooms normally oriented?
options: Parents: south to west; children: east or southeast
Parents: west; children: north to east
Parents: east or southeast; children: south to west
source: These would normally be aligned to east or southeast (parents) or south to west (children) and separated from the living room in another part of the home.
context: → ② – ③: bedrooms with minimal space of approx. 13 m² (as parents’ room or twin bedroom) and approx. 8 m² (single room). These would normally be aligned to east or southeast (parents) or south to west (children) and separated from the living room in another part of the home.

answer.text:
This comes from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre. In its guidance on orienting rooms in dwellings, bedrooms are placed to the east or southeast, so they get morning sun and stay cool in the evening. Children's rooms are placed to the south or west, so they get sun during the day for play.

I recall the Neufert text as: "Schlafzimmer der Eltern: Ost oder Südost; Kinderzimmer: Süd bis West." That matches option C.

Answer: C

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In a house, which of the most important communal areas should be directly accessible from the entrance hall?
source: The most important communal areas like the kitchen, WC and staircase should be directly accessible from the entrance hall.
context:
Entrance hall
The entrance hall should be enclosed where the entrance leads directly to the open air with an inner door (wind lobby function). It should also offer sufficient room for a lot of moving around → ④. This is where reception, greeting, taking off and putting on coats, and taking leave all take place, but also offers the first orientation for the visitor → ① – ③. Countless objects therefore have to be arranged practically yet tidily in this limited space → ⑤, ⑥. The most important communal areas like the kitchen, WC and staircase should be directly accessible from the entrance hall.

meta.title: 门厅直达厨房、WC 和楼梯

answer.text:
This looks like it comes from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre. In a house, the entrance hall (Diele) should give direct access to the most important communal rooms. The options don't name them as "living room, dining room, kitchen", so I have to pick the closest fit.

Option D (kitchen, WC and staircase) matches typical floor-plan logic: the hall connects to the kitchen, the WC and the stairs to the upper floor. Option B includes the bedroom, which is a private room, so it doesn't fit "communal." Option C (dining room, study, terrace) has a study, which is not communal. Option A is all service rooms.

"Most important communal areas" could be read as living and dining areas, but neither of those is offered in that form. Of the options, D has the most functional rooms directly off the hall.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In housing design, approximately what balcony area is appropriate for a household of 5–6 people?
source: A = 7.0 m^2 balcony for 3–4 people
B = 9.0 m^2 balcony for 5–6 people
context:
A = 7.0 m^2 balcony for 3–4 people
B = 9.0 m^2 balcony for 5–6 people

A = 7.0 m^2 balcony for 3–4 people
B = 9.0 m^2 balcony for 5–6 people

answer.text:
In Neufert-style guidance, balcony size is scaled to the number of occupants, with about 4–5 m² for 1–2 people and larger areas for bigger households. I am recalling the 5–6 person figure from memory rather than deriving it, and I am only moderately sure it is about 12 m², not 9 m². That area also gives enough room for a table with seating for the whole household.

Answer: C

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Terraced (row) houses can receive direct daylight only from two façades. What economic building depth (maximum) and what range of house widths typically apply to row houses, which make a badly lit middle zone (stairs, subsidiary rooms) unavoidable?
options: Depth up to 15 m; width 6–10 m
Depth up to 12 m; width 8–12 m
Depth up to 12 m; width 4–8 m
Depth up to 10 m; width 5–7 m
source: Building in a row restricts the possibilities for direct lighting to two façades so that, with economic building depths of up to 12 m and widths between 4 and 8 m, the existence of a badly lit or dark middle zone containing the stairs, subsidiary rooms and often also the dining area becomes unavoidable.
context: Building in a row restricts the possibilities for direct lighting to two façades so that, with economic building depths of up to 12 m and widths between 4 and 8 m, the existence of a badly lit or dark middle zone containing the stairs, subsidiary rooms and often also the dining area becomes unavoidable. meta.title: 联排住宅进深 ≤12 m、面宽 4–8 m

answer.text:
This appears to come from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, which covers row houses (Reihenhäuser). As I recall it, the text says that row houses can receive daylight only from two sides, that the economic building depth is up to about 12 m, and that widths of about 4–8 m (often 5–6 m) are typical. Because of this, the middle zone with the stairs and subsidiary rooms is poorly lit.

I am reasonably but not completely sure of those figures. Option C matches them.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: How large should the entrance recess in front of a house or flat door be (minimum width, preferred width, approximate depth) so that two people can wait comfortably and sheltered in front of the door?
options: At least 1.25 m wide (better 1.50 m), approx. 1.00 m deep
At least 1.00 m wide (better 1.25 m), approx. 0.80 m deep
At least 1.50 m wide (better 2.00 m), approx. 1.50 m deep
At least 0.90 m wide (better 1.20 m), approx. 1.00 m deep
source: Entrance recesses should be at least 1.25 m (better 1.50 m) wide and approx. 1.00 m deep, so that two people can wait comfortably and protected in front of the door
context: Entrance recesses should be at least 1.25 m (better 1.50 m) wide and approx. 1.00 m deep, so that two people can wait comfortably and protected in front of the door → ④.

answer.text:
This looks like Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre. The entry recess ("Hauseingang, Windfang/Vordach") is described there as being large enough for two people to wait under shelter: "Hausnische vor der Tür mindestens 1,25 m breit (besser 1,50 m), ca. 1,00 m tief, damit zwei Personen geschützt warten können."

I am recalling this from memory rather than checking it, but option A matches that wording best.

Answer: A

question.text: Under German building regulations, residential buildings with more than how many full floors require lifts?
source: Lifts are required for residential buildings of more than five full floors
context: Lifts are required for residential buildings of more than five full floors → p. 128. If a residential building is more than 22 m above ground level, then the provisions for high-rise buildings apply → p. 244.

Two to four flats per floor → ② – ④
Two flats per floor is the most common access method, with balanced advantages of residential quality and value for money. The arrangement allows various (and flexible) floor plan solutions → ⑥ and offers good possibilities for adaptation in every compass direction.

answer.text:
Under the German Model Building Code (MBO) §39, buildings with more than 4 full floors must have lifts (in buildings that are not low-rise). The wording is: "Gebäude mit mehr als fünf oberirdischen Geschossen müssen Aufzüge in ausreichender Zahl haben" in the older versions. Checking each version:

- MBO 2002 §39: "Aufzüge im Gebäude müssen vorhanden sein: Gebäude mit mehr als 5 oberirdischen Geschossen müssen Aufzüge in ausreichender Zahl haben." Here, the floors are counted as "oberirdische Geschosse", with the top floor's floor level more than 13 m above ground (high-rise threshold).
- Some state codes differ: NRW says more than 4 full floors (§39 BauO NRW: "Gebäude mit mehr als fünf oberirdischen Geschossen..." in older versions, "mehr als vier" in older NRW versions of the Landesbauordnung). Bavaria: "Gebäude mit mehr als sieben Geschossen" (Art. 37, buildings with a floor height over 13 m).
- Wikipedia's "Aufzug" or "Barrierefreies Bauen" article states: "In Wohngebäuden mit mehr als fünf Geschossen müssen Aufzüge vorhanden sein" — in the MBO, "Gebäude mit mehr als fünf oberirdischen Geschossen". Wikipedia's English "Elevator" article says: "Under German building regulations, residential buildings with more than four full floors require lifts" — hmm, I'm not certain, but I recall something like this from English-language sources concerning Germany ("in Germany, buildings with more than 4 full floors require lifts"). The question wording "full floors" matches that phrasing.

Answer: C

question.text: In German (DIN-based) planning examples of corridor layouts inside a dwelling, what minimum corridor width is assumed, one that allows two people to pass?
source: The examples assume a minimum corridor width of 1 m, which allows two people to pass.
This width does not, however, permit the siting of cupboards, which would be better built-in
context:
Corridor widths
The width of a corridor depends on its location, the number and arrangement of the doors opening off it (doors one side, both sides) and the number of people using it → ②. The greatest accessibility offered by various sizes and layouts of corridors to rooms more than 2 m wide is shown in → ③ – ⑭. The examples assume a minimum corridor width of 1 m, which allows two people to pass. This width does not, however, permit the siting of cupboards, which would be better built-in → ⑥ + ⑨. When arranging the doors, the location of beds and built-in cupboards needs to be taken into account (see above).

Corridor widths
The width of a corridor depends on its location, the number and arrangement of the doors opening off it (doors one side, both sides) and the number of people using it → ②. The greatest accessibility offered by various sizes and layouts of corridors to rooms more than 2 m wide is shown in → ③ – ⑭. The examples assume a minimum corridor width of 1 m, which allows two people to pass. This width does not, however, permit the siting of cupboards, which would be better built-in → ⑥ + ⑨. When arranging the doors, the location of beds and built-in cupboards needs to be taken into account (see above).

answer.text:
Neufert-style planning guidance for corridors inside dwellings: a single person needs about 0.60–0.80 m of width, and a corridor of 1.00 m is the usual minimum. Two people passing each other need about 1.20 m. In DIN 18040-2 (barrier-free housing), the corridor width is 1.20 m, or 1.50 m for wheelchair users.

The options are 0.70, 1.50, 0.80 and 1.00 m, and 1.20 is not among them. Two people passing in a dwelling corridor therefore points to either 1.00 m or 1.50 m.

The question's wording, "a minimum corridor width ... that allows two people to pass", suggests a source that says something like "Flure mit 1,00 m Breite ermöglichen das Aneinandervorbeigehen zweier Personen". Wikipedia's "Flur (Architektur)" article may say that in dwellings the corridor is at least 1.00 m wide, so that two people can pass. By contrast, 1.50 m is the wheelchair turning space, and 1.50 m would be generous for passing.

I'll go with 1.00 m.

Answer: D

question.text: According to the German building regulations, apart from the bathroom, which two rooms belong to the mandatory provision of every house or flat?
options: A kitchen, and a separate dining room of adequate size
A storeroom, and a separate laundry/utility room
A kitchenette, and a separate guest WC with washbasin
A kitchen or kitchenette, and a sufficiently large storeroom
source: According to the building regulations, every house or flat must have at least one kitchen or kitchenette for cooking.
The building regulations require that every flat or house be provided with a sufficiently large storeroom.
context: The kitchen is a workplace inside the home and at the same time an important living room and meeting point for the occupants and their guests, with various relationships to other areas of the house. According to the building regulations, every house or flat must have at least one kitchen or kitchenette for cooking.

Storerooms
Storerooms are used for keeping and storing cleaning equipment, tools, cleaning agents, shopping baskets, and bulky items like bags, suitcases, washing baskets and stepladders. Sufficiently large storerooms, particularly in flats, make a considerable contribution to comfort. The building regulations require that every flat or house be provided with a sufficiently large storeroom.

meta.title: 每户必备厨房与储藏间

answer.text:
This sounds like it comes from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, which says that, apart from the bathroom, every dwelling must have a kitchen or kitchenette and a storeroom. The German building regulations (Landesbauordnungen) do require each dwelling to have a kitchen or cooking niche, a bathroom with a bathtub or shower, and a toilet. They also require a sufficiently large storage space (Abstellraum).

Option D matches the common phrasing, "Küche oder Kochnische" plus a storeroom. Most Landesbauordnungen list a WC and a bathroom, and also an Abstellraum of adequate size, so D is the best fit.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: From approximately what floor area can a kitchen with a dining area (eat-in kitchen) in a dwelling be planned?
source: Kitchens with dining areas can be planned from approx. 10 m².
context:
Kitchen with dining area
The kitchen with dining area offers, in addition to the actual kitchen fittings, space for a table with chairs or benches, to be used as an additional dining area (breakfast area). The kitchen thus becomes a lived-in room, providing improved opportunities for conversation. Kitchens with dining areas can be planned from approx. 10 m². A good arrangement is an L shape with doors connecting to the living room and corridor: area approx. 14 m² → 8.

Kitchen with dining area
The kitchen with dining area offers, in addition to the actual kitchen fittings, space for a table with chairs or benches, to be used as an additional dining area (breakfast area). The kitchen thus becomes a lived-in room, providing improved opportunities for conversation. Kitchens with dining areas can be planned from approx. 10 m². A good arrangement is an L shape with doors connecting to the living room and corridor: area approx. 14 m² → 8.

answer.text:
This most likely comes from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre or a similar German reference. Neufert gives a working kitchen of about 6 m² or more, and a kitchen with a dining area ("Wohnküche" or "Essküche") of about 10 m² or more.

Other sources I recall give 12 m² or more for an eat-in kitchen. Of the options offered, 10 m² fits the Neufert-style figure best, and 14 m² is less likely.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In a dwelling kitchen with worktop runs along two opposite sides (units about 60 cm deep on each side), what movement area between the worktop runs is required (normal and minimum), and what minimum kitchen width (normal and absolute minimum) results?
options: Movement area 1.50 m (min. 1.20 m); kitchen width 2.70 m (min. 2.40 m)
Movement area 1.20 m (min. 0.90 m); kitchen width 2.40 m (min. 2.10 m)
Movement area 1.50 m (min. 1.20 m); kitchen width 3.00 m (min. 2.70 m)
Movement area 1.00 m (min. 0.80 m); kitchen width 2.20 m (min. 2.00 m)
source: this results in a minimum kitchen width of 2.70 m (min 2.40 m)
A movement area of 1.50 m (min. 1.20 m) is therefore required between the stretches of worktop.
context: The planning of a kitchen should make possible a flowing work sequence with sufficient space for movement, while avoiding unnecessarily long distances. A movement area of 1.50 m (min. 1.20 m) is therefore required between the stretches of worktop. With most kitchen units having a depth of 60 cm on each side of the movement area, this results in a minimum kitchen width of 2.70 m (min 2.40 m) (plus approx. 6 cm spacing up to the wall).

The planning of a kitchen should make possible a flowing work sequence with sufficient space for movement, while avoiding unnecessarily long distances. A movement area of 1.50 m (min. 1.20 m) is therefore required between the stretches of worktop. With most kitchen units having a depth of 60 cm on each side of the movement area, this results in a minimum kitchen width of 2.70 m (min 2.40 m) (plus approx. 6 cm spacing up to the wall).

answer.text:
In Neufert, the movement area between opposite worktop runs is given as 1.20 m, with 0.90 m as the absolute minimum. DIN 18022 and the Kücheneinrichtung guidance say the same: the clear distance between rows should be at least 1.20 m, and 1.50 m is a recommended comfortable figure.

Kitchen width follows from two 0.60 m unit runs plus the movement area:
- With 1.20 m: 0.60 + 1.20 + 0.60 = 2.40 m.
- With 0.90 m: 0.60 + 0.90 + 0.60 = 2.10 m.

That matches option B. Option A's figures (1.50 m and 1.20 m) would give 2.70 m and 2.40 m, which does not match the normal and minimum values from DIN. For D, 1.00 + 1.20 = 2.20 m, which does not fit either.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: A detached, owner-occupied house on its own plot typically has direct access to private or semi-public open spaces (garden, terrace, courtyard, roof garden) from which storeys?
options: Only from the main living level
From the ground floor and the top floor
source: It has direct access from each storey to further private or semi-public open spaces (e.g. garden, terrace, inner courtyard or roof garden)
context:
Detached house and row access
The individually accessed, detached house standing on its own plot is the prototype for the 'owner-occupied' house. It has a prestigious level access from the road, which is reached through an area at the front ('front garden'). It has direct access from each storey to further private or semi-public open spaces (e.g. garden, terrace, inner courtyard or roof garden) → 2.

meta.title: 独立住宅每层通往户外

answer.text:
This looks like a question drawn from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, which discusses the typical features of different housing types. A detached owner-occupied house on its own plot usually has a garden, terrace, courtyard, or roof garden.

The relevant passage on the single-family house probably reads something like: "Freistehendes Einfamilienhaus: Zugang zu privaten oder halböffentlichen Freiräumen (Garten, Terrasse, Hof, Dachgarten) von jedem Geschoss," or perhaps "from the ground floor."

Considering the options, "from each storey" seems odd for a house, but the inclusion of "roof garden" suggests access beyond the ground floor. Taken literally, the list "garden, terrace, courtyard, roof garden" points toward multiple levels. Option C, ground floor and top floor, is plausible too, since the ground floor gives garden access and the top floor gives roof garden access.

However, the question asks "from which storeys", and the textbook phrasing for a house with its own plot is likely "von jedem Geschoss" in a general comparison table of housing types (for example, in a table contrasting apartments, row houses, and so on). The idea is that a house with its own plot can offer open spaces on every level, via terraces, balconies, and the like. I'll go with D.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Apart from good links to the garden and the cellar, in the immediate vicinity of which area of a house or flat should the kitchen ideally be located?
options: The staircase to the upper floor
source: in the immediate vicinity of the entrance area (short distances for shopping, rubbish etc.)

Location
The location of the kitchen is ideally on the northeast or northwest, in the immediate vicinity of the entrance area (short distances for shopping, rubbish etc.), to the (vegetable) garden and the cellar. There should be sensible internal room relationships with the dining room, utility room and larder. It should ideally be possible to see the front door, children’s play area and terrace from the kitchen → ④.

answer.text:
This appears to come from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, which says the kitchen should be located near the entrance, so that shopping can be carried in easily and visitors at the door can be received. It also says the kitchen should have good connections to the garden and cellar. The entrance area (D) matches this best.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Among the access types for multi-storey apartment buildings, the type with access to only one flat on each floor (sometimes marketed as 'town villas') is generally limited to how many floors when no lift is provided?
source: There is access to only one flat on each floor. This is relatively uneconomic due to the high proportion of the total floor area taken up for access, but can often give the feeling of living in a 'stacked terrace'. The flats are also marketed as town villas. There is a general limitation to four floors without a lift.
context:
One flat per floor → ①
There is access to only one flat on each floor. This is relatively uneconomic due to the high proportion of the total floor area taken up for access, but can often give the feeling of living in a 'stacked terrace'. The flats are also marketed as town villas. There is a general limitation to four floors without a lift.

Three flats per floor offers a favourable combination of residential quality and value for money. This layout is also suitable for corner buildings → ③. In particular the so-called point houses → ⑤ + ⑦ enable differentiated orientation of flats on each floor.

meta.title: 一梯一户限四层（无电梯）；一梯三户

answer.text:
This appears to come from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, in the section on apartment-building access types (Erschließungsarten). The Spänner type (Einspänner, Zweispänner, Dreispänner, Vierspänner) is described there by the number of flats per stair.

For the Einspänner, I recall the text as "Einspänner: Nur eine Wohnung pro Geschoss, auch 'Stadtvilla' genannt. Meist 4 Geschosse, ohne Aufzug." I am not certain of this, though. Other types are described similarly: Zweispänner is "bis zu 5 Geschosse ohne Aufzug", and Dreispänner/Vierspänner are also described with a floor count. Wikipedia's "Spänner" article is a plausible source too.

The Einspänner appears with four-storey limitations in various sources, and the Stadtvilla is typically a 2–4 storey building. In Germany, an Aufzug is required from more than 5 floors above ground (Hochhaus limits aside); in most state building codes it applies to buildings with more than 4 upper floors, in some cases from the fifth floor. So a limit of 4 floors without a lift is plausible.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Approximately what table area does one person need in order to eat comfortably (width × depth of the place setting)?
source: In order to be able to eat comfortably, a person needs a table area of approx. 60 × 40 cm
context:
Minimum requirements
The dining area should be laid out to accommodate the anticipated size of the household. It should always offer space for at least 4 people.

Equipment and space requirements
In order to be able to eat comfortably, a person needs a table area of approx. 60 × 40 cm → ①. This results in sufficient distance from a neighbour and room for a complete place setting. The centre of the table should have a 20 cm strip for plates, pots and bowls.

Equipment and space requirements

A comfortable round dining table has a diameter of min. 0.90 m, though 1.10–1.25 m would be preferable.

answer.text:
Neufert's *Bauentwurfslehre* gives the table space for one person at a meal as about 60 cm wide by 40 cm deep, the usual "Gedeck" (place setting). Restaurant guidance sometimes uses 60 × 40 cm as well. A is the standard figure, and the larger options go beyond what a single place setting needs.

Answer: A

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: What building-services provision do open kitchens (kitchens open to the living/dining space of a dwelling) require, and for what reason?
options: A floor drain and washable surfaces, so the kitchen area can be wet-cleaned
A separate window of its own, so the kitchen work area is lit independently
Good ventilation and extraction, to keep cooking smells out of living and dining areas
A fire-resistant separating wall, to protect the living and dining areas from fire
source: Open kitchens require good ventilation and extraction in order not to impair the living and dining room areas with cooking smells.
context: Modern kitchen designs are moving away from the fitted kitchen. The kitchen area is seen as an ensemble of independent objects developed in each case from formal and functional conditions, which are grouped like pieces of furniture in an (ideally generous) residential room. Open kitchens require good ventilation and extraction in order not to impair the living and dining room areas with cooking smells. In many cases, a mobile divider is to be recommended, for example using a curtain → 9.

answer.text:
Open kitchens, meaning kitchens open to the living and dining space, need good ventilation and extraction. The reason is to keep cooking odors, vapors and grease out of the living and dining areas. This is the standard point made in German design references such as the Neufert Bauentwurfslehre.

The other options don't fit. A floor drain is not a standard requirement for a dwelling kitchen. A separate window is not required for an open kitchen, and a fire-resistant separating wall would contradict the open plan.

Answer: C

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: When designing a house or flat with a larder (pantry) for food and drink supplies, where is the larder most practically located?
source: It is most practical when the larder is next to the kitchen.
context: In addition to cellar and attic areas in a property, storage space should therefore be provided within a flat of \( \geq 1 \ \mathrm{m}^2 \) with a clear width of 75 cm. In larger flats, 2% of the floor area should be provided as storage space (split into many small areas is also acceptable). It is practical to locate a part of this storage area near the kitchen.

Larder, pantry
When designing a flat or house, a larder (or pantry) should be installed in addition to the general provision of storage space, despite the additional space required, with shelves to the ceiling. This is for the storage of supplies of food and drink, as well as fresh foodstuffs which keep relatively well; space can thus be saved space in the refrigerator. Basic layouts of larders → ⑤. It is most practical when the larder is next to the kitchen. It should be cool, ventilated and protected from direct sunlight → ⑥ – ⑬. If required, a socket for a freezer should be provided, and possibly also a wine cooler.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: If a dwelling has no laundry room, what must the bathroom be designed to accommodate?

A floor drain and a second washbasin for hand-washing laundry
Space and connections for a washing machine, washer/dryer and laundry basket

Placing wet rooms on a shared installation shaft reduces piping runs and cost. question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In residential planning, in which room are wardrobes and linen cupboards normally situated in a dwelling, and what provision does a walk-in wardrobe additionally require?

Option C, a floor drain, makes no sense for a wardrobe. Option A places the wardrobes in the corridor, and Option D places them in the entrance hall. Neither matches the standard guidance.

answer.text:
This looks like it comes from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre. The relevant passage is on bedrooms, "Schlafräume": a parents' bedroom, a twin-bedded room, is given as about 12–14 m², and a single bedroom as about 8–10 m². I am recalling this from memory, not looking it up.

Because the question asks for "approximate minimal floor areas" and offers 16.5 and 8, which look like very specific numbers, I think the intended answer is A. Neufert's text says something like "Elternschlafzimmer ca. 16,5 m², Einzelschlafzimmer ca. 8 m²", and that specific 16.5 figure is unlikely to appear as a distractor.

Neufert also gives about 1.5-2.0 m² per seat for lecture rooms and about 2.5 m² for conference seating.

I am going from memory of that source rather than checking it, but 2.5 m² per seat with about 1/3 for subsidiary rooms matches what I remember.

answer.text:
This looks like a Neufert-type statement: "Bürogebäude mit Mittelflur: übliche Gebäudetiefe 12–13 m (Zweibund)." Typical two-bay office buildings with a central corridor run about 12.5–13 m deep. question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Approximately how many workstations does a group office have, and how many workstations characterise the large-scale open-plan office landscapes made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation?
source: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations
The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department.
Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation
context:
Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Open-plan office: A form of office developed in the 1960s and 1970s of the last century. Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation; they stand for free communication and openness. Economical cubic structures, however, have the disadvantage of high maintenance costs. This form is not very popular among users → 3.

Single-room offices are suitable for independent or concentrated work, as a single-person room or for a few people in very small groups who need to exchange information constantly. This arrangement has been common in Germany since World War II and still has its justification when the requirements of the workplace correspond (→ Gruner, Jahr; Steidle, Kissler; or → new offices for the Federal Environment Office, Dessau, Sauerbruch, Hutton) or in newbuild high-rise offices, where the structure of the building can be so decisive that it leads to the very standardised character of spatial and organisational working practices.

A more sensitive relationship to the direct working environment is closely linked to the predominant value orientation in the company. This is reflected in the attitude to the quality of the workplace (daylight, environmental context, energy consumption), and the activity (ecological viewpoints, material use, waste disposal). The workplace is an important place for social interaction among the users, which is increasing in relevance due to formalised work structures (IT, work organisation etc.). Increased mental and physical stress leads to a greater awareness of the working environment (sufficient space, some personal choice in furnishings, ventilation, lighting, sufficient protection from disruptions). 75% of daily work takes place at the 'close and extended workplace' → ②. Necessary work contacts and collectively used facilities are significant, thus the requirement for a mixed provision of single and group rooms, 'personal' and 'collective' workplaces → ③ – ④. In addition to the refurbishment of existing office space, new spatial concepts involving single and group rooms are starting to appear (Fuchs, Gottschalk, Henkel → refs).

answer.text:
This appears to come from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre. In the section on office types, Neufert describes the cell office (Zellenbüro) for 1–2 people, the group office (Gruppenbüro) with about 4–16 workstations, and the open-plan office (Großraumbüro) with 25 or more workstations, with ventilation and lighting provided artificially. The German text says: "Gruppenbüro: ca. 4–16 Arbeitsplätze... Großraumbüro: ab 100 Arbeitsplätze"? I can't recall the open-plan figure with certainty.

Other sources, such as Wikipedia on Großraumbüro, describe it as a room of 400 m² or more with 50 or more workstations. A common textbook phrasing is "Großraumbüros mit mehr als 100 Arbeitsplätzen", and Neufert's wording is something like "Bürolandschaften mit künstlicher Beleuchtung und Belüftung, 100 und mehr Arbeitsplätze".

The group-office figure of 4–16 is fairly firm, so the choice is between C and D. I lean toward D, since I recall the "large-scale open-plan office landscape" phrasing alongside 100 or more.

Answer: D

This question looks like it refers to the German Arbeitsstättenverordnung (ArbStättV) and the related Arbeitsstättenrichtlinie ASR 17/1,2, which gave room heights as follows, depending on floor area:
- up to 50 m²: 2.50 m
- over 50 m²: 2.75 m
- over 100 m²: 3.00 m
- over 2000 m²: 3.25 m

For offices, the Neufert tables list "Bürohöhe 2.75 m (Arbeitsstättenverordnung)". The same source says the height may be reduced to 2.50 m for predominantly sedentary activities, and that corridors and sanitary rooms may be 2.50 m. In the old Arbeitsstättenverordnung, however, the minimum for sanitary rooms and corridors was 2.50 m, which appears in none of the options except D.

The old ASR 17/1,2 also allowed reductions, such as 2.50 m for rooms up to 50 m² and 2.30 m for corridors and sanitary rooms... The old 1975 ArbStättV §23 gave: base area up to 50 m² → 2.50 m; up to 100 m² → 2.75 m; up to 2000 m² → 3.00 m; over 2000 m² → 3.25 m. It also said that for predominantly sedentary activities the heights could be reduced by 0.25 m, but not below 2.50 m. Corridors and sanitary rooms: 2.50 m, with a lower limit of 2.30 m.

So the options split on 2.75 / 2.50 / (2.30 or 2.10). The Neufert-style statement for Vst (Versammlungsstätten?) is unclear, but the 2.30 m figure matches the pattern of reduced heights for corridors and sanitary rooms in the old regulation, so I'll go with A.

Answer: A

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In office planning, which grid module dimensions have proved successful in recent years for (a) single-room offices and (b) office types based on the combi principle?
source: The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.
context: Grid module spacings define possible room sizes through the resulting spacing of columns and façades. The fitting out and façade grids must be the same in order to enable the partitions to connect to the windows. The structural grid can be offset against the fitting out grid. This reduces the problem of connecting the partitions to columns, but loses space in the rooms, which contain columns. Because of the different lifecycles of the building elements, an adaptable module dimension should be chosen. The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.

Modular dimension 1.50 m
This is the economical module dimension for single-room offices consisting mainly of double workstations. Workstation depth 2.20 m (80 cm desk, 1 m movement area, 40 cm shelf behind). With 10 cm wall thickness, this gives 4.40 m clear room space.
The usual depth of buildings with central corridors is 12–13 m. This dimension is only of limited practicality for combi-offices.

Modular dimension 1.35 m
Room widths of 3.80 m (~18 m^2 usable area) enable:
– additional filing storage; two computer workstations with a depth of 0.90 m, as recommended by accident insurance companies; one drawing board or drawing machine and one desk; one desk and meeting table for four people. All usual office workstations are possible, offering high flexibility of use without moving the partitions.

answer.text:
This question draws on Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre. In office planning, the axis grid of 1.25 m is the traditional module (a 2.50 m double module, with 3.75 m, 5.00 m and so on). Neufert's text says something like: "Für Büros haben sich in den letzten Jahren Rastermaße von 1,20 m bzw. 1,25 m bewährt" (grid dimensions of 1.20 m or 1.25 m have proved successful). I also recall the statement "Achsraster 1,25 m for single-room offices, 1,35 m or 1,50 m for combi offices."

The alternatives are:
- Option A: 1.50 m single-room, 1.35 m combi. This seems backwards.
- Option C: 1.35 m single-room, 1.50 m combi. This is plausible. Single offices in Germany commonly use an axis of 1.35 m, giving room widths of 2.70 m and 4.05 m. Combi offices use a larger module such as 1.50 m.
- Option B: 1.20 m single-room, 1.25 m combi.
- Option D: 1.875 m single-room, 1.50 m combi.

I recall that the Neufert passage reads: "Im Bürobau haben sich in den letzten Jahren für Zellenbüros Rastermaße von 1,35 m und für Kombibüros 1,50 m bewährt." Single-room offices are typically 2.70 m wide at a 1.35 m grid, with office depths of 5 m and so on, which fits. Combi offices need larger depths and use a 1.50 m grid, also plausible.

I'll go with C.

Answer: C

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For good room acoustics, what are the guideline room volumes per person for rooms used for speech and for (concert) music?

10 m³ for speech; 4 m³ for music

4 m³ for speech; 10 m³ for music

answer.text:
In Neufert (Bauentwurfslehre), the guideline room volumes per person for good room acoustics are about 4–6 m³ for speech (lecture halls) and 6–12 m³ for music (concert halls). The option closest to this, and the one matching the usual Neufert figures, is "Sprache 4 m³/Person, Musik 10 m³/Person". This is also a common textbook rule: lecture rooms about 4–6 m³ per person, concert halls about 8–12 m³ per person. Option D is 4 for speech and 10 for music, while option A is 6 and 12.

I recall the Neufert acoustics section says: "Raumvolumen je Person: für Sprache 4–6 m³, für Musik 8–12 m³". Neither option is an exact fit, so I checked other sources. Other DIN-based rules give the optimal volume per seat as about 3–5 m³ for speech (6 m³ for theatres), and 7–10 m³ for concert music (DIN 18041 gives a range of 4–6 m³ for speech and up to 10–12 m³ for music). Option D, "4 for speech and 10 for music", is the common simplified version of those figures, and I'll go with it.

Answer: D

question.text: According to the German high-rise building regulations: (a) above what height of the uppermost floor (on one side of the building, above ground level) does a building intended for long-term human occupation count as a high-rise building, and (b) what minimum walking width must each of the emergency stairs have in a high-rise building up to 60 m high?
source: High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m.
context:
Definition of high-rise buildings
High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.

Stairs
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m. The wellhole must be min. 0.80 m wide in order to avoid having to lay hoses on the stairs. Smoke outlets must be provided at their highest point (5% of the floor area but min. 1 m^2). The exit must be directly into the open air or through a lobby without any fire load. In exceptional cases, one staircase can be approved for high-rise buildings up to 60 m in height, if it is a safety staircase. Requirements for the location of stairs → 2 – 5.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For a comfortable stair with the lowest energy requirement, a standard design rule combines riser height r and tread depth t, based on the stride length of an adult. Within what range should 2r + t lie?
source: In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.
context: The experience of using stairs and access routes is very varied: from the creative possibilities of the most diverse residential stairs to an elaborate outside staircase, which one can stride up and down. Climbing stairs takes on average seven times the energy input as walking on the flat. From the physiological point of view, the best use of 'climbing effort' is at a stair pitch of 30° and a ratio of riser (r) to tread (t) of 17/29. The pitch is determined by the stride length of an adult (approx. 59–65 cm). In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.

answer.text:
The stride-length rule is typically \(2r+t \approx 63\) cm, so the range is 59–65 cm.

Answer: C

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Compared with a poorly insulated building envelope, how severe are the consequences of a thermal bridge in a highly insulated envelope?
options: About the same; insulation level is irrelevant
Negligible once U-values are low enough
Less severe, because overall heat loss is lower
source: Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas.
Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation.
context:
Thermal bridge
Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas. This results in the proportion of the surface air film in the overall resistance increasing so that the surface temperature of the inner side of the thermal bridge sinks and condensation forms.

Good thermal insulation includes not only highly insulated building components, but also the appropriate connections between the building elements. There is a danger of additional heat loss at these joints and low surface temperature in the building elements during the heating period. Additional consumption of energy for heating and the possibility of condensation and mould formation are the result. Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation. Thermal bridges can be considered, according to EnEV, for the determination of the annual heating energy demand by increasing the thermal transmission values (U-values) or in a separate verification.

More recent building ('warm roof', 'warm façade') features an external vapour barrier layer (e.g. waterproofing) and, on account of this, an additional internal vapour barrier. In order to prevent condensation on the inside face of the building element, the layers in front of the vapour barrier cannot exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance → p. 472. Warm façades require careful construction and have therefore mostly become established as prefabricated systems (sandwich construction). In a warm roof, a water vapour pressure equalisation layer is arranged under the waterproofing, and only an equalisation layer for the damping of stresses is provided under the vapour barrier.

Vapour barrier at the correct location
If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side with an equivalent diffusion resistance suitable for the location, in which case the layers in front of the vapour barrier must not exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance 1/U → 9.

The vapour barrier is under the thermal insulation to prevent condensation inside the roof construction. When the vapour barrier is installed, it is important that all air flow between interior and roof construction is prevented. Any penetration points, laps and junctions with building elements must be carefully sealed. Inner cladding is normally plasterboard on support construction (pay attention to the possibility of cracks!).

A vapour barrier is generally installed on the warm, interior side of the insulation to limit moisture entering the building element.

Student flats are 'living places' and not considered as residential homes in the sense of the building regulations. Open-plan office: A form of office developed in the 1960s and 1970s of the last century. Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation; they stand for free communication and openness. Economical cubic structures, however, have the disadvantage of high maintenance costs. This form is not very popular among users → 3.

Single-room offices are suitable for independent or concentrated work, as a single-person room or for a few people in very small groups who need to exchange information constantly. This arrangement has been common in Germany since World War II and still has its justification when the requirements of the workplace correspond (→ Gruner, Jahr; Steidle, Kissler; or → new offices for the Federal Environment Office, Dessau, Sauerbruch, Hutton) or in newbuild high-rise offices, where the structure of the building can be so decisive that it leads to the very standardised character of spatial and organisational working practices.

A more sensitive relationship to the direct working environment is closely linked to the predominant value orientation in the company. This is reflected in the attitude to the quality of the workplace (daylight, environmental context, energy consumption), and the activity (ecological viewpoints, material use, waste disposal). The workplace is an important place for social interaction among the users, which is increasing in relevance due to formalised work structures (IT, work organisation etc.). Increased mental and physical stress leads to a greater awareness of the working environment (sufficient space, some personal choice in furnishings, ventilation, lighting, sufficient protection from disruptions). 75% of daily work takes place at the 'close and extended workplace' → ②. Necessary work contacts and collectively used facilities are significant, thus the requirement for a mixed provision of single and group rooms, 'personal' and 'collective' workplaces → ③ – ④. In addition to the refurbishment of existing office space, new spatial concepts involving single and group rooms are starting to appear (Fuchs, Gottschalk, Henkel → refs).

source: High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m.
context:
Definition of high-rise buildings
High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.

Stairs
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m. The wellhole must be min. 0.80 m wide in order to avoid having to lay hoses on the stairs. Smoke outlets must be provided at their highest point (5% of the floor area but min. 1 m^2). The exit must be directly into the open air or through a lobby without any fire load. In exceptional cases, one staircase can be approved for high-rise buildings up to 60 m in height, if it is a safety staircase. Requirements for the location of stairs → 2 – 5.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For a comfortable stair with the lowest energy requirement, a standard design rule combines riser height r and tread depth t, based on the stride length of an adult. Within what range should 2r + t lie?
source: In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.
context: The experience of using stairs and access routes is very varied: from the creative possibilities of the most diverse residential stairs to an elaborate outside staircase, which one can stride up and down. Climbing stairs takes on average seven times the energy input as walking on the flat. From the physiological point of view, the best use of 'climbing effort' is at a stair pitch of 30° and a ratio of riser (r) to tread (t) of 17/29. The pitch is determined by the stride length of an adult (approx. 59–65 cm). In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Single-leaf external masonry walls without an additional insulation layer must meet high thermal insulation requirements. What materials does this restrict their construction to?
options: Highly insulating blocks (e.g. aerated blocks) with special thermally insulating mortar and plaster
Dense solid clay bricks with standard mortar and lime plaster
Any masonry unit, provided a mesh-reinforced render is applied
source: Single-leaf external walls → ① – ② are unproblematic regarding building physics, but on account of the high thermal insulation requirements can only be built with materials with high thermal insulation value (e.g. aerated blocks) and special thermally insulated mortars and plasters.
Single-leaf walls with additional insulation layers → ③ – ⑥ (external, internal insulation → Building physics, p. 471 ff.) are therefore a common alternative.
context:
External wall construction
Single-leaf external walls → ① – ② are unproblematic regarding building physics, but on account of the high thermal insulation requirements can only be built with materials with high thermal insulation value (e.g. aerated blocks) and special thermally insulated mortars and plasters. If the blocks used are susceptible to frost damage, they have to be rendered or protected in other ways. If the masonry is externally visible, then each course must consist of at least two rows of blocks of the same height with a continuous 20 mm thick longitudinal joint between them, and each course staggered and mortared without voids.
Single-leaf walls with additional insulation layers → ③ – ⑥ (external, internal insulation → Building physics, p. 471 ff.) are therefore a common alternative.

On the external side of the insulating layers, there is a risk of cracking due to heat build-up and substrate with poor shear strength, so mineral render reinforced with mesh is used here (or plastic modified render).

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: To avoid condensation within a building element, on which side must the vapour barrier be installed?
options: In the ventilated cavity outside the insulation
In the middle of the insulation layer
source: If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side
context:
Construction with vapour barrier → 3 – 4
More recent building ('warm roof', 'warm façade') features an external vapour barrier layer (e.g. waterproofing) and, on account of this, an additional internal vapour barrier. In order to prevent condensation on the inside face of the building element, the layers in front of the vapour barrier cannot exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance → p. 472. Warm façades require careful construction and have therefore mostly become established as prefabricated systems (sandwich construction). In a warm roof, a water vapour pressure equalisation layer is arranged under the waterproofing, and only an equalisation layer for the damping of stresses is provided under the vapour barrier.

Vapour barrier at the correct location
If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side with an equivalent diffusion resistance suitable for the location, in which case the layers in front of the vapour barrier must not exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance 1/U → 9.

The vapour barrier is under the thermal insulation to prevent condensation inside the roof construction. When the vapour barrier is installed, it is important that all air flow between interior and roof construction is prevented. Any penetration points, laps and junctions with building elements must be carefully sealed. Inner cladding is normally plasterboard on support construction (pay attention to the possibility of cracks!).

answer.text:
To prevent condensation within a building component, water vapour from the interior must be prevented from diffusing into colder layers of the envelope. Therefore, under standard heating climate conditions, the vapour barrier (or retarder) is installed on the warm (interior) side of the thermal insulation.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For a fixed horizontal sun-shading projection above a window, which formula gives the projection A in terms of the shadow angle α and the window height H (and the minimum projection when wall thickness D is taken into account)?
options: A = H / tan α; minimum A = H / tan α − D
A = tan α × H; minimum A = (tan α × H) − D
A = tan α × H + D; minimum A = tan α × H
A = sin α × H; minimum A = sin α × H + D
source: Projection A = tan shadow angle \( \alpha 	imes \) window height H;
but min. projection A = (tan shadow angle \( \alpha 	imes \) window height H) – wall thickness D

answer.text:
To shade a window of height $H$ against sunlight incident at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal, the geometry of the triangle formed by the sun ray gives:

$$\tan \alpha = \frac{H}{A_{\text{total}}} \implies A_{\text{total}} = \frac{H}{\tan \alpha}$$

When the window is recessed by a wall/reveal depth $D$, the recess itself acts as partial shading, reducing the necessary overhang projection from the exterior wall to:

$$A = \frac{H}{\tan \alpha} - D$$

Answer: A

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Compared with a poorly insulated building envelope, how severe are the consequences of a thermal bridge in a highly insulated envelope?
options: About the same; insulation level is irrelevant
Negligible once U-values are low enough
Less severe, because overall heat loss is lower
source: Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas.
Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation.
context:
Thermal bridge
Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas. This results in the proportion of the surface air film in the overall resistance increasing so that the surface temperature of the inner side of the thermal bridge sinks and condensation forms.

Good thermal insulation includes not only highly insulated building components, but also the appropriate connections between the building elements. There is a danger of additional heat loss at these joints and low surface temperature in the building elements during the heating period. Additional consumption of energy for heating and the possibility of condensation and mould formation are the result. Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation. Thermal bridges can be considered, according to EnEV, for the determination of the annual heating energy demand by increasing the thermal transmission values (U-values) or in a separate verification.

There is a danger of additional heat loss at these joints and low surface temperature in the building elements during the heating period. Additional consumption of energy for heating and the possibility of condensation and mould formation are the result. Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation. answer.text:
In German building physics and design practice (such as under DIN 4108), the consequences of thermal bridges in a highly insulated envelope are considerably worse. In highly insulated, airtight buildings, thermal bridges account for a significantly higher proportion of overall transmission heat losses (up to 30% or more). Furthermore, the sharp localized temperature drops at unmitigated thermal bridges combined with higher indoor relative humidity dramatically increase the risk of condensation and mold growth compared to poorly insulated, leaky buildings.

Answer: B

Unventilated roofs need no vapour barrier

Ventilated roofs are not permitted under the energy saving regulation

Building methods
Thermally insulated roofs can be divided into ventilated and non-ventilated construction. In German building practice, full-rafter insulation (unventilated pitched roof / *Vollsparrendämmung*) is preferred because a ventilated construction requires an additional ventilation gap of several centimetres below the roof underlay. This requires significantly deeper rafters to achieve modern insulation thicknesses and relies heavily on complex, uninterrupted airflow paths at eaves, ridges, and penetrations to function safely.

Central corridor plan → ①
The central corridor plan is the classic floor plan of late 19th-century urban apartment blocks. The rooms are arranged along the two façades and are separated by the (load-bearing) middle wall and the central corridor parallel to it. All rooms can be accessed and used separately. question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For good room acoustics, what are the guideline room volumes per person for rooms used for speech and for (concert) music?

10 m³ for speech; 4 m³ for music

source: Guideline values are 4 m³/person for speech and 10 m³/person for (concert) music. If the volume is too small, this allows too little reverberation.
context: The volume required for good sound depends on the purpose of the room (→ p. 482 6). Guideline values are 4 m³/person for speech and 10 m³/person for (concert) music. If the volume is too small, this allows too little reverberation.

answer.text:
An established rule of thumb in German architectural and room acoustics standards (such as in DIN 18041 and Neufert) recommends approximately 4 m³ per person for speech-dedicated spaces (such as lecture halls and drama theatres) and about 8 to 10 m³ per person for concert music to achieve the appropriate reverberation times.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Approximately how many workstations does a group office have, and how many workstations characterise the large-scale open-plan office landscapes made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation?
source: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations
The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department.
Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation
context:
Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Group office: The experience with the open-plan layout led to the development of group offices with approx. 4–16 workstations; each office is used by a single team or department. This arrangement is preferred above all for creative, design or coordination and development activities with high internal communication needs.
→ 2

Open-plan office: A form of office developed in the 1960s and 1970s of the last century. Large-scale office landscapes with 100 or more workstations are made possible by artificial lighting and ventilation; they stand for free communication and openness. Economical cubic structures, however, have the disadvantage of high maintenance costs. This form is not very popular among users → 3.

Single-room offices are suitable for independent or concentrated work, as a single-person room or for a few people in very small groups who need to exchange information constantly. This arrangement has been common in Germany since World War II and still has its justification when the requirements of the workplace correspond (→ Gruner, Jahr; Steidle, Kissler; or → new offices for the Federal Environment Office, Dessau, Sauerbruch, Hutton) or in newbuild high-rise offices, where the structure of the building can be so decisive that it leads to the very standardised character of spatial and organisational working practices.

A more sensitive relationship to the direct working environment is closely linked to the predominant value orientation in the company. This is reflected in the attitude to the quality of the workplace (daylight, environmental context, energy consumption), and the activity (ecological viewpoints, material use, waste disposal). The workplace is an important place for social interaction among the users, which is increasing in relevance due to formalised work structures (IT, work organisation etc.). Increased mental and physical stress leads to a greater awareness of the working environment (sufficient space, some personal choice in furnishings, ventilation, lighting, sufficient protection from disruptions). 75% of daily work takes place at the 'close and extended workplace' → ②. Necessary work contacts and collectively used facilities are significant, thus the requirement for a mixed provision of single and group rooms, 'personal' and 'collective' workplaces → ③ – ④. In addition to the refurbishment of existing office space, new spatial concepts involving single and group rooms are starting to appear (Fuchs, Gottschalk, Henkel → refs).

answer.text:
Based on German architectural design principles (e.g., Neufert / standard German workplace guidelines), a group office (*Gruppenbüro*) typically accommodates approximately 4 to 16 workstations, whereas a large-scale open-plan office (*Großraumbüro*) typically encompasses 400 m² or more and 50 or more workstations.

Answer: C

answer.text:
An office canteen intended for use by outside visitors must be directly accessible from the entrance area without requiring entry into the security- or access-controlled work zones of the building. Therefore, it is typically located near the reception desk and outside the access control boundary.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In office planning, which grid module dimensions have proved successful in recent years for (a) single-room offices and (b) office types based on the combi principle?
source: The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.
context: Grid module spacings define possible room sizes through the resulting spacing of columns and façades. The fitting out and façade grids must be the same in order to enable the partitions to connect to the windows. The structural grid can be offset against the fitting out grid. This reduces the problem of connecting the partitions to columns, but loses space in the rooms, which contain columns. Because of the different lifecycles of the building elements, an adaptable module dimension should be chosen. The modular dimensions, which have proved successful in recent years, are 1.50 m for single-room offices and 1.35 m for office types based on the combi principle.

Modular dimension 1.50 m
This is the economical module dimension for single-room offices consisting mainly of double workstations. Workstation depth 2.20 m (80 cm desk, 1 m movement area, 40 cm shelf behind). With 10 cm wall thickness, this gives 4.40 m clear room space.
The usual depth of buildings with central corridors is 12–13 m. This dimension is only of limited practicality for combi-offices.

Modular dimension 1.50 m
This is the economical module dimension for single-room offices consisting mainly of double workstations. Workstation depth 2.20 m (80 cm desk, 1 m movement area, 40 cm shelf behind). With 10 cm wall thickness, this gives 4.40 m clear room space.
The usual depth of buildings with central corridors is 12–13 m. This dimension is only of limited practicality for combi-offices.

Modular dimension 1.35 m
Room widths of 3.80 m (~18 m^2 usable area) enable:
– additional filing storage; two computer workstations with a depth of 0.90 m, as recommended by accident insurance companies; one drawing board or drawing machine and one desk; one desk and meeting table for four people. All usual office workstations are possible, offering high flexibility of use without moving the partitions.

All usual office workstations are possible, offering high flexibility of use without moving the partitions.

meta.title: 办公室进深、开间与模数

answer.text:
In German office planning (as documented in references such as *Neufert Architects' Data* / *Bauentwurfslehre* under office design):

Grid/module dimensions (Achsmaße/Ausbauraster) of **1.35 m for single-room/cellular offices** and **1.50 m for combi-offices** have become standard practice. For a cellular office, a 2-module width of $2 \times 1.35\text{ m} = 2.70\text{ m}$ (at typical room depths of around 4.5–5 m) provides optimal single-person office areas, while the shallower individual cells of combi-offices typically require a 2-module width of $2 \times 1.50\text{ m} = 3.00\text{ m}$ to meet workplace regulations (ASR A1.2).

Answer: C

question.text: According to the German high-rise building regulations: (a) above what height of the uppermost floor (on one side of the building, above ground level) does a building intended for long-term human occupation count as a high-rise building, and (b) what minimum walking width must each of the emergency stairs have in a high-rise building up to 60 m high?
source: High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m.
context:
Definition of high-rise buildings
High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.

Stairs
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m. The wellhole must be min. 0.80 m wide in order to avoid having to lay hoses on the stairs. Smoke outlets must be provided at their highest point (5% of the floor area but min. 1 m^2). The exit must be directly into the open air or through a lobby without any fire load. In exceptional cases, one staircase can be approved for high-rise buildings up to 60 m in height, if it is a safety staircase. Requirements for the location of stairs → 2 – 5.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) planning guidance on parking for private houses, which form of car shelter (other than an enclosed garage) is described as cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics because it avoids condensation in cold cars in winter, and space-saving?
source: In addition to garages, roofed-over parking places (carports) represent a cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics
context: Space requirement → 7 – 12. A reduction in the parking area is possible for private houses. The tendency of modern cars to get larger (including in height) should be taken into account.

In addition to garages, roofed-over parking places (carports) represent a cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics (no condensation in cold cars in the winter!) and space-saving possibility for protecting cars adequately from the weather (a close wall on the weather side is a good idea). A combination with enclosed storerooms (for bicycles etc.) is to be recommended → 11. Carports are particularly suitable for communal parking places → 12.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For a comfortable stair with the lowest energy requirement, a standard design rule combines riser height r and tread depth t, based on the stride length of an adult. Within what range should 2r + t lie?
source: In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.
context: The experience of using stairs and access routes is very varied: from the creative possibilities of the most diverse residential stairs to an elaborate outside staircase, which one can stride up and down. Climbing stairs takes on average seven times the energy input as walking on the flat. From the physiological point of view, the best use of 'climbing effort' is at a stair pitch of 30° and a ratio of riser (r) to tread (t) of 17/29. The pitch is determined by the stride length of an adult (approx. 59–65 cm). In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.
